nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Common Snook
Scientific Name: Centropomus undecimalis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
       Class: Osteichthyes
       Order: Perciformes
       Family: Centropomidae

nodes.title: Subspecific Names
nodes.body:
Synonyms: The following synonyms are listed by Jordan and Evermann (1518).
 	Sciaena undecimalis (Bloch1792)
 	Centropomus undecimradiatus (Lacepede1802)
 	Sphyraenna  aureoviridus (Lacepede 1803)
 	Centropomus  appendiculatus (Poey 1860)
  	Centropomus  undecimalis (Cuvier and Valenciennes 1828)
Other Common Names: Gulf pike, salt water pike (327), robalo (327 1293), robalo comun (302 600), thin snook (432 633), robalo blanco (791), sergeant fish (1294).

nodes.title: Taxonomic Characteristics
nodes.body:
Egg: Fertilized eggs are spherical, yellowish-white in color with transparent yolk material containing a single well defined oil globule ranging from 0.17 to 0.30 mm in diameter (6 40 404).  Hatching rates reported in laboratory experiments are 16-18 h at 28 C and 24 to 30 h at 27.8 to 30.6 C.  Fertilized eggs float in salt water >20 % (6 404 734).

Larvae: 1.4 to 1.5 mm SL at hatching with large yolk sac, large oil globule in anterior most portion of yolk sac, and transparent finfold present around most of body (404 734).  Increase to ca. 2.1 mm SL by 36 h after hatching (AH) (404).  At this time eyes are becoming pigmented, mouth begins to develop, yolk sac absorbed, gut increases in diameter and is partitioned (404).  Eyes and jaws complete 32 to 48 h AH and digestive system function by 72 h AH (636 734).  Larvae 2.2 to 2.3 mm SL at approximately 96 h AH with oil globule completely absorbed and swimbladder visible above gut.  Notochord flexion begins from 3.6 to 3.8 mm SL and is usually complete by 4.5 mm.  Caudal fin visible by 3.2 mm SL; pelvic fin buds visible between 5.0 to 5.5 mm SL; pelvic girdle completely ossified by 8.6 mm SL and heavily lined with teeth.  Larval stage ends with scale development at 13.8 to 16.4 mm SL, 34 days AH (404).

nodes.title: Young-Of-Year
nodes.body:
Juvenile: Almost entire caudal skeleton ossified by 21.9 mm SL, and by 26.4 mm SL melanophores begin to form along lateral line darkening it and the fins (404).  Juveniles have appearance of small adults at this point.  Between 35 and 40 mm SL, first anal ray transforms into third anal spine (404).  Adult:  Fusiform pike-like body silver coloration, with distinct black lateral line; high divided dorsal fin; sloping forehead; large mouth, protruding lower jaw; growth much larger than other snooks; pelvic fins yellow (1502).
Similar Species: Tarpon Snook (C. pectinatus), Swordspine Snook (C. ensiferus), Fat Snook
(C. parallelus) in Florida (788) and Puerto Rico (1480).

nodes.title: Stock Separation
nodes.body: Note: Reference for Scientific Name is (Bloch)

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Overall: From New York to Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, occurring along the eastern coast of central America, throughout the Caribbean, along the Gulf coast from Mexico to Port Aransas, Texas, and along peninsular Florida from Santa Rosa Co. to Volusia Co. and the St. Johns River (6 40 132 157 327 432 465 600 734 783 788).  Rare north of Florida but reported as strays in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Delaware and New York (414 422 440 465 1297 1298).  Centers of abundance occur in the Caribbean, southwestern Gulf of Mexico, and mangrove belts of southern Florida (235 515 734).  Habitat requirements and temperature are probably the most important factors determining the range of snook in U.S. waters (6 132 327 432 1068).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Florida: Common year-round in coastal bays, estuaries, and lower reaches of streams and rivers along the southern Florida peninsula from Indian River Lagoon and Tampa Bay south through the Keys and Tortugas (235 264 265 432 568 599 743 790 1299).  Rare on the Gulf coast north of Tampa Bay, but they have been reported from Destin (1299).
By Stock: Mitochondrial DNA analysis was conducted on 120 common snook from 5 estuaries in Florida and compared to samples from Costa Rica and Venezuela (1479).  Costa Rican and Venezuelan samples were related and more similar to Florida west coast samples that to east coast samples.  C. pectinatus, C. parallelus, and C. ensiferus were more genetically similar to each other than to C. undecimalis, probably because they occupy riverine habitats whereas the common snook tends to occupy estuarine habitats.  The analyses indicate common snook on the east and west coasts of Florida could be managed separately.
By Estuary: Present in the following west Florida estuaries: Florida Bay, Ten Thousand Islands, Caloosahatchee River, Charlotte Harbor, Tampa Bay, Suwannee River, Appalachia Bay, and Apalachicola Bay (1501).  On the east coast of Florida common snook are found in Indian River Lagoon (235) others?
Spatial Strategy: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic and planktonic (6 734).  As snook mature into juveniles and adults they become pelagic and nektonic (414 481 734). Juveniles and adults usually found in schools (79 734). All stages exhibit diurnal activity.
A relatively non-migratory, inshore species (481 743 633 1484).  Apparently has a broad inshore range and moves freely in this area as conditions permit in short coastwise movements (481 734).  Most juvenile snook in the Little Manatee River were taken along the shoreline of two marginal creek/cove sites (1492).  Most juvenile snook in Tampa Bay were concentrated in two tributaries (the Alafia and Little Manatee Rivers) (1485).  Adult snook were also concentrated in tributaries, except in the spring when they were scattered throughout nearshore areas of Tampa Bay.
Mobility/Migration (by life stage):
Movements from estuaries and fresh water tributaries to spawning areas just offshore can be considered a limited spawning migration (481 734).  Juveniles exhibit a habitat specificity which changes as the fish grow older resulting in localized movements; adult habitat requirements are not as narrow as those of juveniles although limited movement occurs throughout the life cycle (235).
Eggs and early larvae: Are pelagic and planktonic (6 734).
JUVENILE/ADULT: As snook mature into juveniles and adults they become pelagic and nektonic (414 481 734). All stages exhibit diurnal activity.

Symbiotic: No evidence of symbiosis
Schooling: Juveniles and adults usually found in schools (79 734).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body: Substrate: Juveniles and adults have been found over bottoms of clay, mud, mud-sand, sand, sand with rocks, detritus with mud and sand, and sand with shell (70 79 264 265 432 456).

nodes.title: Intertidal Bottom
nodes.body:
Vegetation:  The preferred habitat, mangrove and salt marshes, are not extensive in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico, which along with the need for relatively warm temperatures, probably accounts for the relative scarceness of this species.  This habitat is similar to that of the tarpon, Megalops atlanticus, which, like the snook, is declining in numbers, giving support to the hypotheses of habitat destruction and/or environmental change as common causes for their disappearance (132 327 432 515 599).


Submerged Vegetation (by life stage):
Larvae Peters (1476) found early larval stages in open water, and post larval snook (5-7 mm SL) in shallow water nursery habitats in Tampa Bay and Dollar Bay (near Naples Florida).  Larvae, collected in the summer in Naples Bay, were found to be associated with the bottom (1301).  Larvae settle onto mangrove prop-roots.  An attempt to simulate mangrove prop-roots with cubic meter artificial floating habitats was considered ineffective for snook larvae (1481).  However, the bundles did attract 8-15 mm TL snook larvae when sunk to the bottom.  After  66 d 8 remained and had grown to 70 mm TL.

nodes.title: Young-Of-Year
nodes.body:
Egg and larvae: Shallow open waters of river mouths, beach inlets and passes, and estuarine passes in polyhaline to euhaline salinities (6 404 414 481 568 636 734 743).  Raised in the laboratory in euhaline salinities but can survive and develop in freshwater at 14 d after hatching (404 636 734).  Larvae probably hatch in shallow open waters off beaches, inlets, and passes, and make their way inshore to estuary nursery grounds (414 432 743).
Juvenile: Prefer protected bodies of water usually of small surface area and shallow water depth when small (664), and seagrass beds when larger (235).  Shoreline vegetation is also considered a possible important element as juveniles also occur in areas with vegetation other than seagrass (456).  Collected in ditches, tidal pools, headwaters of creeks, ponds, bays, estuaries, and shorelines in freshwater to euhaline salinities at depths from one to four feet (6 40 72 157 265 279 327 414 422 432 440 456 465 664 702).  In SW Florida, Fore and Schmidt (1301) found that primary nursery areas were brackish, shallow, warm tidal streams and dredged canals with slow currents and soft bottoms with little submerged vegetation, but often with shoreline stands of red or white mangroves. McMichael et al. (456) described a similar habitat for juvenile snook in the Tampa Bay area.  The type of vegetation present did not seem to be as important as the physical protection provided in the form of overhanging or partially submerged branches or grass that provided physical cover in areas along shorelines with a relatively steep dropoff (1493).  Gilmore et al. (235) described three distinct habitat types on the Florida east coast: freshwater tributaries, salt marshes, and seagrass beds as primary snook nursery areas.  Young move from shallow riverine habitat to deeper water or bays as they grow (235).

Management, habitat protection, and restoration continues to be inadequately funded (1488).  Lewis emphasized the need for nursery protection, restoring normal season water flows to estuaries, and habitat restoration as underutilized tools in snook fishery management.  Geographic information systems (GIS) technology is being used to assess changes in fisheries habitat, the effects of urbanization, and increasing fishing pressure on snook and other species (1486).

Efforts to restore wetlands were conducted, through wetland mitigation, water quality, and circulation improvements with a 1500 acre man made estuary in Broward County Fl (1474).  Snook abundance from 1986-1989 compared to 1992 did not increase.  Efforts to restore water quality in Tampa Bay resulted in reductions in nutrient input (1489).  The 1993 phytoplankton production was near half the rates measured in the early to mid 1980`s.  The recolonization of seagrass was minor.  A substantial reduction in fisheries yields may have resulted from the decrease in primary production.
Adult: Found in estuaries, Gulf passes, channels, beaches, river mouths, mangrove or salt marshes, ponds, brackish coastal waters, streams, and lakes (6 40 264 302 327 395 432 515 633 702 934 1303).  Reported in waters from 0.3 to 3.66 m in depth ranging in salinity from fresh water to euhaline (35 132 264 395).

Depth Distribution: Needs information.

nodes.title: WATER COLUMN HABITAT
nodes.body:
Temperature: Very responsive to temperature with detrimental effects occurring at approximately 15 C or less (235 432).
Egg: No eggs have been observed in the wild, but they have been successfully spawned and developed at 28 C (404 636 734 1302 1309).  Experiments evaluated the development of eggs at 24, 26, 29 and 32 C (1490).  Development rates increased with increasing temperature.
Larvae: Larvae propagated in laboratories have been successfully raised at 24.6 to 32.4 C (404 636 734 1302) Larvae have been collected from Naples Bay, Florida in temperatures ranging from 28.7 to 31.4 C (1301).   In the laboratory all larvae reared at 24 C died (1490).  Statistical evaluation of developmental stages a t 26, 29, and 32 C indicated that 26 C resulted in the greatest larval growth and maximum yolk utilization efficiency.  The acute upper temperature tolerance of post-hatch larvae and the effects of initial acclimation temperature were investigated (1495).  Two day post-hatch larval mortalities increased from 30, 32, and 37 C, with 100% mortality at 34 C after 15 h. Similar results were found with 6-d post-hatch larvae.  Lower initial rearing temperatures resulted in lower maximum temperature tolerated.
Juvenile/Adult: Found in waters with a temperature range of 14.2 to 35.6 C (132 157 264 414 432 440 456 465 637 664 702).  In laboratory experiments, juveniles stopped feeding at 14.2 C, lost equilibrium at 12.7 C and died at 12.5 C (637).  More recent experiments found the lower lethal temperature for Florida snook ranged from 9 C in saltwater (19 %) to 10 C in freshwater (1408). The lower lethal limit for juveniles has been reported as 12 to 14 C, while that of adults probably approaches the lower end of a 6 to 13 C range suggesting adults are somewhat more tolerant of colder temperatures than fingerlings (236 264 432 637 664 1023 1068 1408).    McLaughlin et al. (1493) stated that juvenile snook did not seem to be adversely affected by colder water temperatures, which cause adult mortality.  Howells et al. (1408) suggested that other parameters (stock origin, food, salinity, and fish size) probably contributed to the differences in lower lethal temperatures observed in the various studies.  Numerous authors have reported snook as lethargic or stunned as a result of winter freezes (6 132 236 264 432 1023 1068). Gunter (253) reported that 6800 kg of snook and drum were killed near the southern tip of Texas during a severe winter in 1940, and Storey and Gudger (1068) listed snook as a species killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg/Larvae: Eggs and larvae have been raised in the lab in salinities from 30 to 38 % (404 636 734).  Both appear to prefer polyhaline to euhaline salinity ranges and are unable to develop in fresh water.  Larvae at 14 days of development can be successfully transferred to fresh water and are considered euryhaline at this point (6 636).  Snook larvae have been collected in Naples Bay, Fl at salinities ranging from 14.8 to 33.5 % (1301).  Salinities of >20 % are necessary to activate sperm for successful spawning (6 636).
Juvenile/Adult: Euryhaline, reported from a salinity range of 0.0 to 36 % (80 132 157 235 264 265 304 395 432 440 456 664 702 703).  On the Florida east coast, juveniles <50mm consistently occur at lower salinities whereas those >150mm are generally found in higher salinity habitats (235).  Snook are relatively widespread in freshwater (790) and have been collected in Lake Okeechobee (1313), coastal rivers (264 265), the Big Cypress Swamp (395), and at several locations in the Everglades (395 515 599 702).  Physiological studies of juveniles indicate they can osmoregulate at salinities between 0 and 45 % in a manner similar to other brackish water fishes (1311).  More than 70% of seine-caught and 90% of trawl-caught specimens taken in the Little Manatee River from 1988 to 1991 were taken at salinities <5 % (1492).  Maximum numbers were taken in October and November.  Changes in blood osmolality and gill morphology of juvenile snook after acclimation at various salinities (0, 15, 30, and 40 %) was investigated (1473).  The study found that juveniles quickly adapted to sudden changes in salinity.  The chloride cells in the gill appeared to be metabolically active regardless of salinity.

nodes.title: Dissolved Oxygen
nodes.body:
Egg and Larvae: No information available.
Juvenile: Juvenile snook have been collected in impound wetland habitats associated with the Indian River Lagoon with D.O. levels of less than 1.0 mg/l (1271).  Peterson and Gilmore (1466) found an ontogenetic change in a juvenile snook`s ability to survive reduced oxygen levels, which correlated well with the habitat shift noted by Gilmore (235).  Small juveniles may also use aquatic surface respiration to utilize the well-oxygenated surface film during hypoxic events (1467).
Adult: No information available.
Turbidity: No data available.

nodes.title: Trophic Mode
nodes.body:
Feeding (by life stage):
Food Items: (by life stage)
Larvae: Considered stenophagous.  Planktivore preying chiefly on copepods and their eggs and larvae.  Also feed on other invertebrate eggs, crab zoae, foraminifera, algae, and plant tissue (279).  Laboratory reared larvae began feeding when 2-3 days old and accepted rotifers, newly hatched Artemia, and copepod nauplii between 53 and 130 microns in size (1309).  Late post-larvae also feed on neonatal Gambusia (235 1309).
Juvenile: Data from wild-caught juveniles indicate that feeding occurs during the daytime (456).
 Smaller individuals have been reported as having eaten small copepods, amphipods, mysids, and zoaea and adults of palaemonid shrimp (80 235 279 456 664 1314 1491).  A feeding transition apparently occurs when juveniles are about 45mm long (456).  Snook become piscivorous at 25 to 30 mm TL with fish constituting the major portion of diet by 56 mm SL (279 636 664 1303).  Food organisms include: Anchoa mitchilli; Lagodon rhomboides; Gambusia affinis, Gambusia holbrooki, Cyprinodon variegatus; Palaemonetes spp., Penaeus spp., plant tissue, insects, and fish (235 279 456 1303 1491).  The predator-prey behavior of juvenile snook was studied in the laboratory (1491).
Adult: Diet consists mostly of fish and shrimp, but crabs, crayfish, and some plant tissue also utilized (279 432 1303 1314).  Fish constitute the most important component with the following reported from diet studies: Brevoortia sp., Eucinostomis sp., Mugil cephalus, Mugil sp., Lagodon rhomboides, Lagodon sp., Anchoa sp., Orthopristes chrysopterus, Poecilia latipinna, Gambusia affinis, Gambusia sp., and Molliensia sp. (80 432 515).

nodes.title: Mode
nodes.body:
Domain: Snook spawn in higher saline estuarine and marine environments.  Fish ready to  spawn congregate in schools in shallow, saline, open waters just offshore in such areas as: river mouths, estuarine passes, along open beaches in the vicinity of inlets with actual spawning most likely in shallow nearshore waters (6 79 235 414 432 481 743).

Fertilization: Oviparous, external fertilization, sexes separate, exhibits sex reversal (1471).  Comparisons of the chromosomes of males and females did not show differences in chromosomatic size or number.  The banding patterns on the chromosomes supported the hypothesis of protandric hermaphroditisn.  Examination of more than 4,100 snook gonads confirmed that snook undergo sex reversal (1478).  For all snook <= 500 mm and < age 4 the sex ratio was skewed in favor of males (6.1 M:1.0 F), whereas for fish >= 800 mm and > age 7 the sex ratio favors females (1.0M: 3.2F).
Spawning Strategy:  broadcast spawner, eggs were most abundant in Tampa Bay during late evening and early morning hours (1499).
Reproductive Periodicity: Mating and spawning occurs in Florida from May to mid-November with peak spawning periods from June t o July along the southeast and southwest coasts and in August along the East central coast (6 235 432 456 481 734 743 1303). However, some spawning may occur year round in the warmer parts of the range. One female with roe reported from Corpus Christi, Texas in July (35); a ripe female was collected in early May in Haiti (40).

A diel and lunar sampling protocol was used to determine peak periods of various reproductive activities in Tampa Bay (1499).  Catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) and the gonadosomatic index (GSI) were highest during the new moon period of June and July.  Snook eggs from plankton samples were first present in Tampa Bay on June 7.

nodes.title: Seasonal Energetics
nodes.body:
Parental Care: No guarding of eggs or larvae takes place (1499).
Maturation: Several studies have examined the sizes and ages of sexual maturity by sex of snook (327 432 600 788 1477).  Some snook mature by the end of the second year, but most are not mature until the end of the third year upon reaching a FL of 500 mm (432 743). The minimum reported sizes at maturity are 337 mm FL for females and 338 mm FL for males with approximately 50% mature at 400 mm and virtually all mature at 500 mm (432). The most comprehensive study found predicted sizes and ages at 50% maturity for east coast fish were males 379 mm at 2.3 yr, females 644 mm at 3.7 yr, and on the west coast males 401 mm at 1.9 yr, females 499 mm FL at 2.6 yr (1477)
Fecundity: Spawns large numbers of eggs; a 584 mm FL female contained ca. 1,440,000 eggs (743), and a 795mm female contained ca. 1,648,000 eggs (40).  Fecundity has been tentatively estimated at 45,000 eggs/lb body weight with some fractional spawning being reported (6 432).
Development (by life stage):

nodes.title: GROWTH
nodes.body:
Length Range:(by life stage)
Egg: Fertilized eggs are 0.68-0.73 mm in diameter (6, 40, 404)
Larvae: At hatching 1.4 to 1.5 mm SL, increases to ca. 2.1 mm SL by 36 h after hatching (AH) (404). The larval stage ends at 13.8 to 16.4 mm SL, 34 days AH.

nodes.title: Young-Of-Year
nodes.body:
Juvenile: Minimum size described 13.8 mm SL (404).  Juveniles are 163 mm FL at the end of the first winter (743).
Adult: The maximum size observed for male snook was 925 mm FL, and female snook was 1105 mm FL in Florida (1475).  Average size of adult is 91 cm TL with a weight of 4.5 kg, but can reach 1232 mm TL and 24.3 kg (327 788 600).

nodes.title: Length At Age
nodes.body:
Larvae: Growth rate for larvae varies.  Newly hatched larvae at 28+/-1 C grow 1.02 mm/day for a few hours, slowing rapidly to ca. 0.15 mm/day when about 2.4 mm SL.  Growth rate then increases gradually with increasing size from 0.15 to 0.50 mm/day in snook between 3.5-22.0 mm SL (404).
Juvenile: Recorded growth rate for juveniles in the wild is 0.5-1.2 mm/d (235 456) with a reported average of 0.6-0.7 mm/d for the first eight months of life (456).  Juveniles are 163 mm FL at the end of their first winter, and 342 mm FL by the end of their second (743).
Adult: The age and growth of snook was compared between the east and west coasts (1475).  Atlantic coast fish grow more quickly and reach a larger size sooner than snook on the Gulf coast.  The average size for males at age 13 was 812 mm FL on the east coast and 810 mm on the west coast of Florida  The average size for female snook was 1025 mm FL at age 18 on the east coast and 947 mm at age 19 on the west coast of Florida
Longevity:   Males live 13 yr, females 19 yr (1475).
Growth Equations: McMichael et al (456) found the following equations were good predictors of growth for summer-spawned juveniles:
[eq]
      A = 2.903488(L) - 0.024782(L^2) + 0.000096(L^3);   r^2 = 0.99
      	L = 0.008610(A^2) - 0.000025(A^3);                 r^2 = 0.99
[/eq]
where A is the age in days and L is standard length in mm.

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Important commercial fish in Central and South America, particularly in Mexico and Venezuela (791).  Never an important commercial species in the US, and in the early 20th century it was considered as barely edible (1294) and reported to be of little value at Key West (846).  By 1917, some fish were reaching commercial markets in the Fort Myers area where fish houses paid $.04/lb for snook (1068).  Demand developed early in Louisiana and in Texas it was considered as one of the important species in the 1930`s (35 432).  Caught on a small scale, Texas landings peaked at 105,451 lbs in 1928, and Florida landings peaked in 1948 at 800,698 lbs (432 446).  Declining numbers led to a ban on commercial landings in Florida in 1958 and to its virtual disappearance in Texas with the last commercially landed fish occurring there in 1961 (35 302 304 432 446 734 743).  Snook were taken infrequently by gill nets in Tampa bay (1494).
Recreational: Regarded as a popular sportfish, putting up spectacular fights as well as being good eating (6 35 327 432 440 633 736 734 743 788 791).  Readily accepts natural or artificial bait on hook and line; it is also caught by spearing (791).  Population declines since the 1930`s have resulted in this fish rarely being taken by sportsmen in Texas where it accounts for <1% of sport landings (304 446 734). Common snook landings in Florida in 1994 totaled 103,937 fish and were relatively evenly split between the Atlantic and Gulf coasts (1500).
Ecological Role: Considered a high trophic level carnivore feeding mostly on fish (279 636 664).  Juveniles use periferal habitats, including wetland impoundments, as nursery areas and may be an important transport mechanism to move energy out of these systems (235 1272).
Management Status: The commercial fishery for snook in Florida.ended in 1957, when the Florida Legislature banned all sales of snook, and granted the species gamefish status (1496).   The sport fishery is regulated through the Florida Marine Fisheries Commission (FMFC).  A saltwater recreational fishing license is required, if fishing from a boat at depths greater than four feet.  The holder of a marine sport fishing license and a snook stamp may land two snook per day.  Hatchery programs to enhance snook populations through stocking are discussed in the STOCK ENHANCEMENT description.
Species Stress: None.

nodes.title: Status
nodes.body: Stock Status: Snook stocks on the east and west coasts of Florida have been increasing.

nodes.title: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
nodes.body:
Induced Breeding: Collection of wild broodstock for hatchery production was accomplished on most days during the new moon (June-July) period (1504).  Success in induced spawning in Florida occurred during 1988 when the fish were captured in the afternoon after maturation of oocytes had commenced in wild-caught snook.

Six cell types have been identified in the adenohypophysis of adult snook (1505).  The somatotropic (STH) and gonadotropic (GTH) cells showed marked staining and morphological differences between winter and summer. Ager et al. (6) described the artificial spawning and development of Florida snook eggs and larvae during 1974 and 1975.  Maturation was induced using human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG).  Milt stored at 40 F up to 12 h was satisfactory for fertilization.  Injections of testosterone and leutenizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) during 1988 had some effect on maturation of males but not female snook in Texas (1506).  Attempts to induce maturation using increasing temperature (26 to 30 C) and increasing photoperiod (12h to 15h light period) in Texas were unsuccessful in inducing maturation (1507).  Attempts to induce maturation of snook maintained in cages in ponds were also unsuccessful (1508).

Three field spawning methods were tested in Florida during 1987 (1509).  Source spawning of fish captured early in the day and held in net pens resulted in 5 out of 143 fish spawned naturally. No fish spawned in net pens after field capture during the evening.  With fish given HCG injections, 2 out of 12 (16.7%) produced viable spawns.  Quasi-domesticated snook maintained on a long photoperiod (16 h) at 30 C ad 32 % salinity became mature and were spawned during 1989-91(1510).   Wild-caught fish maintained under the same conditions did not become sexually mature.  Stress minimization appeared to be the key to successful spawning.

A successful protocol for HCG-induced spawning of field-collected snook was developed in Florida during 1989 and 1990 (1514).  The most successful time was 32 to 34 h after HCG injection.  A seawater-free milt collection and storage system was developed.  The viability of eggs increased by obtaining eggs by excision rather than manual stripping of sexually mature adult snook.  Techniques for induced maturation and spawning were described by Roberts (1515).
Rearing: Lack of agitation of the water in rearing tanks during the first 6 h of incubation proved critical for consistent embryo development (6).   Hatching occurred from 24-30 h at temperatures between 82-87 F.  Poor fingerling survival precluded evaluation of reduced salinity on growth of juvenile snook in culture ponds in Texas during 1988 (1511).  Some fingerling production in Texas was achieved using fertilized eggs produced by FDNR with the eggs obtained from strip spawned broodfish (1512).  Eggs incubated at 27-29 C and 31-38 % for 2.5 d yielded 660,000 fry.  Some success was achieved by stocking fry into fertilized earthen ponds.  After 133 d, 1,665 fingerling snook averaging 133 mm TL were recovered for a survival rate of 53.7%.  Hence, snook fingerlings were produced in Texas ponds using techniques developed for rearing red drum.  Earlier studies in Florida have demonstrated excellent survival and growth of fingerling and subadult snook when stocked in sub-tropical freshwater ponds (1513).

Despite notable progress in producing fertilized eggs in Florida, the production of fry in large numbers by 1995 was still a hit and miss operation (1516).  The variable survival of different batches of fry may be due to a virus such as vibrato, or unknown water quality requirements.   It has been proposed that high larval mortalities may be due to a deficiency of unsaturated fatty acids (HUFAs) in the diets of culture fry (1517).
Feeding: An experiment was conducted with different diet combinations: 1) the algae Nannochloropsis oculata fed to rotifers; 2) Trochofeed (Pacific oyster trochophores); 3) Bioencapsulated food (oil emersion); 4) soybean meal; 5) Microfeast (modified fermentation product); and 6) zooplankton (collected wild).   Feeds were introduced when 50% of the larvae exhibited peristaltic movement.  Growth rates varied widely between replications of the same diet. The best growth 0.08 mm/d) occurred with the Nannochloropsis fed rotifer diet.  Ingredients that produced the best survival of larvae (5-7 d post-hatch) were the rotifer diet, bioencapsulation, soybean meal and trochophores.
Stocking: Due to the problems with producing juvenile snook in hatcheries, little or no research has been conducted to evaluate survival after stocking into marine environments.
Disease Control:   The monogenean, Rhabdosynochus rhabdosynochus present on the gills of adult snook broodstock was controlled by trichlorofon (dylox) at 1 mg/l (1469).  Rapid reinfestation of broodstock after treatment suggests that monogenean eggs may be resistant to the chemical.  A 5-7 d bath with 10 mg/l nitrofurazone promoted healing and inhibited bacterial growth and abrasions on hatchery held snook.

nodes.title: POPULATION
nodes.body: Total Mortality: Total mortality (Z) and Actual mortality (A) rates have been determined from frequencies at age for common snook from Tampa Bay, and near Naples on the west coast, and from the Jupiter-Lake Worth Inlets on the east coast of Florida (1475, 1503).  The calculations derived from catch curves were done for the sexes separately and for the sexes combined.  The Z for Tampa Bay (1995) across ages 3-8 was 0.646 for the sexes combined (1503).  The Z for Naples Bay (1976-1981) across ages 4-8 was 0.687, and for the Jupiter-Lake Worth area (1995) was 0.476 across ages 6-14 for the sexes combined.  This is equivalent to Actual mortality rates (A) of 48% for Tampa Bay, 50% for Naples Bay, and 38% for Jupiter-Lake Worth.

nodes.title: Natural Mortality
nodes.body: Fishing Mortality: No hooking mortality was noted with 23 adults monitored with ultrasonic transmitters (1483).  The hooking mortality was evaluated in terms of lure type, hook position, and water temperature (1487).  The total mortality out of 234 snook caught and released was 2.1%.  The mortalities from being hooked on the gill, hooked in the mouth, foul-hooked, and gut hooked were 0%, 0.81%, 0.21% and 17% respectively (R. Taylor, pers. comm. 1996).  No deaths were recorded for snook taken with lures.

nodes.title: Abundance By Month
nodes.body:
Abundance By Year: The trend in recreational angler total-catch rates (CPUEs) has been upward since 1985 on the Atlantic coast, and since 1987 on the Gulf coast (1500).  The kept-catch rates have remained fairly stable since about 1985 on both coasts of Florida  Fishery independent estimates of common snook abundance in Tampa Bay and in Jupiter/West Palm Beach Inlets also indicate increasing trends since 1990 (1477).
Population Abundance: Tag-recapture methods were used to estimate trends in snook population abundance in Jupiter and Lake Worth inlets on the east coast, and in two microhabitats near Port Manatee in Tampa Bay on the west coast of Florida (1475).  East coast estimates were about 14,000 in 1990 and 1991, and then increased to 35,866 in 1992.  Length frequencies indicated a 16% increase on the east coast during 1992.

nodes.title: Annual Cohort Success
nodes.body:
Management Regulations (by state and federal):
Florida: A decline in sport catches in the late 1970`s and early 1980`s and tagging data indicating a population decline, induced the Florida Legislature to grant emergency power to the Florida Dept. of Nat. Res. (FDNR) in 1982 to institute a closed season on the sport fishery.  Stringent management in recent years, combined with mild winters, may have influenced increases in snook abundance.   Current Florida laws include a closed season from 15 December through January and during June-August, a minimum 24� TL, a 2 fish bag limit, and allow possession of only one fish larger than 34�TL.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Competition: Interactions with other species include habitat overlapping and parasitism.  Possible competition may exist between snook and associated fish such as Megalops atlanticus, Elops saurus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Bairdiella chrysoura, and Centropristes ocyurus (414).

nodes.title: Predation
nodes.body: Parasites/Diseases:  An unidentified nematode has been reported parasitizing the mesentery and stomach wall of snook, but apparently with no ill effects (432).  Other reported parasites are Philometra centropomi in the nasal mucosa (633) and Prosthenhystera obesa in the gall bladder (1312).  Snook have also been identified as a host for Lymphocystis virus (633).  Gill ectoparasites have also been described (1308).  Three species of myxosporidian parasites found in snook are Myxobolus centropomi (n. sp.), Ceratomyxa choleospora (n. sp.), and Fabeospora sp.(1468).  Other parasites found on snook include a monogenean (Rhabdosynochus rhabdosynochus), digenean (Lecithochirium microstomum), nematodes (Dichelyne spinicaudatus, Contracaecum spiculigerum),  and a copepod (Caligulus pretextus).

nodes.title: Eutrophication
nodes.body: Pollutant Toxicity: Environmental factors are believed to have played a large role in addition to fishing mortality in the decline in snook populations in various areas of Florida (432 1496 1497 1498).  Environmental alterations and degradations include reduced freshwater inflow to estuaries, sewage and industrial pollution, dredging and filling, mosquito control practices and pesticide use.  Malathion and baytex, pesticides commonly used in mosquito control, were found to be toxic to snook eggs and larvae (1498).  There were birth defects in larvae exposed to malathion.

sections.heading: Taxonomic Characteristics
sections.content:
Egg: Fertilized eggs are spherical, yellowish-white in color with transparent yolk material containing a single well defined oil globule ranging from 0.17 to 0.30 mm in diameter (6 40 404).  Hatching rates reported in laboratory experiments are 16-18 h at 28 C and 24 to 30 h at 27.8 to 30.6 C.  Fertilized eggs float in salt water >20 % (6 404 734).

Larvae: 1.4 to 1.5 mm SL at hatching with large yolk sac, large oil globule in anterior most portion of yolk sac, and transparent finfold present around most of body (404 734).  Increase to ca. 2.1 mm SL by 36 h after hatching (AH) (404).  At this time eyes are becoming pigmented, mouth begins to develop, yolk sac absorbed, gut increases in diameter and is partitioned (404).  Eyes and jaws complete 32 to 48 h AH and digestive system function by 72 h AH (636 734).  Larvae 2.2 to 2.3 mm SL at approximately 96 h AH with oil globule completely absorbed and swimbladder visible above gut.  Notochord flexion begins from 3.6 to 3.8 mm SL and is usually complete by 4.5 mm.  Caudal fin visible by 3.2 mm SL; pelvic fin buds visible between 5.0 to 5.5 mm SL; pelvic girdle completely ossified by 8.6 mm SL and heavily lined with teeth.  Larval stage ends with scale development at 13.8 to 16.4 mm SL, 34 days AH (404).

sections.heading: Young-Of-Year
sections.content:
Juvenile: Almost entire caudal skeleton ossified by 21.9 mm SL, and by 26.4 mm SL melanophores begin to form along lateral line darkening it and the fins (404).  Juveniles have appearance of small adults at this point.  Between 35 and 40 mm SL, first anal ray transforms into third anal spine (404).  Adult:  Fusiform pike-like body silver coloration, with distinct black lateral line; high divided dorsal fin; sloping forehead; large mouth, protruding lower jaw; growth much larger than other snooks; pelvic fins yellow (1502).
Similar Species: Tarpon Snook (C. pectinatus), Swordspine Snook (C. ensiferus), Fat Snook
(C. parallelus) in Florida (788) and Puerto Rico (1480).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content: Overall: From New York to Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, occurring along the eastern coast of central America, throughout the Caribbean, along the Gulf coast from Mexico to Port Aransas, Texas, and along peninsular Florida from Santa Rosa Co. to Volusia Co. and the St. Johns River (6 40 132 157 327 432 465 600 734 783 788).  Rare north of Florida but reported as strays in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Delaware and New York (414 422 440 465 1297 1298).  Centers of abundance occur in the Caribbean, southwestern Gulf of Mexico, and mangrove belts of southern Florida (235 515 734).  Habitat requirements and temperature are probably the most important factors determining the range of snook in U.S. waters (6 132 327 432 1068).

sections.heading: By State
sections.content:
Florida: Common year-round in coastal bays, estuaries, and lower reaches of streams and rivers along the southern Florida peninsula from Indian River Lagoon and Tampa Bay south through the Keys and Tortugas (235 264 265 432 568 599 743 790 1299).  Rare on the Gulf coast north of Tampa Bay, but they have been reported from Destin (1299).
By Stock: Mitochondrial DNA analysis was conducted on 120 common snook from 5 estuaries in Florida and compared to samples from Costa Rica and Venezuela (1479).  Costa Rican and Venezuelan samples were related and more similar to Florida west coast samples that to east coast samples.  C. pectinatus, C. parallelus, and C. ensiferus were more genetically similar to each other than to C. undecimalis, probably because they occupy riverine habitats whereas the common snook tends to occupy estuarine habitats.  The analyses indicate common snook on the east and west coasts of Florida could be managed separately.
By Estuary: Present in the following west Florida estuaries: Florida Bay, Ten Thousand Islands, Caloosahatchee River, Charlotte Harbor, Tampa Bay, Suwannee River, Appalachia Bay, and Apalachicola Bay (1501).  On the east coast of Florida common snook are found in Indian River Lagoon (235) others?
Spatial Strategy: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic and planktonic (6 734).  As snook mature into juveniles and adults they become pelagic and nektonic (414 481 734). Juveniles and adults usually found in schools (79 734). All stages exhibit diurnal activity.
A relatively non-migratory, inshore species (481 743 633 1484).  Apparently has a broad inshore range and moves freely in this area as conditions permit in short coastwise movements (481 734).  Most juvenile snook in the Little Manatee River were taken along the shoreline of two marginal creek/cove sites (1492).  Most juvenile snook in Tampa Bay were concentrated in two tributaries (the Alafia and Little Manatee Rivers) (1485).  Adult snook were also concentrated in tributaries, except in the spring when they were scattered throughout nearshore areas of Tampa Bay.
Mobility/Migration (by life stage):
Movements from estuaries and fresh water tributaries to spawning areas just offshore can be considered a limited spawning migration (481 734).  Juveniles exhibit a habitat specificity which changes as the fish grow older resulting in localized movements; adult habitat requirements are not as narrow as those of juveniles although limited movement occurs throughout the life cycle (235).
Eggs and early larvae: Are pelagic and planktonic (6 734).
JUVENILE/ADULT: As snook mature into juveniles and adults they become pelagic and nektonic (414 481 734). All stages exhibit diurnal activity.

Symbiotic: No evidence of symbiosis
Schooling: Juveniles and adults usually found in schools (79 734).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content: Substrate: Juveniles and adults have been found over bottoms of clay, mud, mud-sand, sand, sand with rocks, detritus with mud and sand, and sand with shell (70 79 264 265 432 456).

sections.heading: Intertidal Bottom
sections.content:
Vegetation:  The preferred habitat, mangrove and salt marshes, are not extensive in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico, which along with the need for relatively warm temperatures, probably accounts for the relative scarceness of this species.  This habitat is similar to that of the tarpon, Megalops atlanticus, which, like the snook, is declining in numbers, giving support to the hypotheses of habitat destruction and/or environmental change as common causes for their disappearance (132 327 432 515 599).


Submerged Vegetation (by life stage):
Larvae Peters (1476) found early larval stages in open water, and post larval snook (5-7 mm SL) in shallow water nursery habitats in Tampa Bay and Dollar Bay (near Naples Florida).  Larvae, collected in the summer in Naples Bay, were found to be associated with the bottom (1301).  Larvae settle onto mangrove prop-roots.  An attempt to simulate mangrove prop-roots with cubic meter artificial floating habitats was considered ineffective for snook larvae (1481).  However, the bundles did attract 8-15 mm TL snook larvae when sunk to the bottom.  After  66 d 8 remained and had grown to 70 mm TL.

sections.heading: Young-Of-Year
sections.content:
Egg and larvae: Shallow open waters of river mouths, beach inlets and passes, and estuarine passes in polyhaline to euhaline salinities (6 404 414 481 568 636 734 743).  Raised in the laboratory in euhaline salinities but can survive and develop in freshwater at 14 d after hatching (404 636 734).  Larvae probably hatch in shallow open waters off beaches, inlets, and passes, and make their way inshore to estuary nursery grounds (414 432 743).
Juvenile: Prefer protected bodies of water usually of small surface area and shallow water depth when small (664), and seagrass beds when larger (235).  Shoreline vegetation is also considered a possible important element as juveniles also occur in areas with vegetation other than seagrass (456).  Collected in ditches, tidal pools, headwaters of creeks, ponds, bays, estuaries, and shorelines in freshwater to euhaline salinities at depths from one to four feet (6 40 72 157 265 279 327 414 422 432 440 456 465 664 702).  In SW Florida, Fore and Schmidt (1301) found that primary nursery areas were brackish, shallow, warm tidal streams and dredged canals with slow currents and soft bottoms with little submerged vegetation, but often with shoreline stands of red or white mangroves. McMichael et al. (456) described a similar habitat for juvenile snook in the Tampa Bay area.  The type of vegetation present did not seem to be as important as the physical protection provided in the form of overhanging or partially submerged branches or grass that provided physical cover in areas along shorelines with a relatively steep dropoff (1493).  Gilmore et al. (235) described three distinct habitat types on the Florida east coast: freshwater tributaries, salt marshes, and seagrass beds as primary snook nursery areas.  Young move from shallow riverine habitat to deeper water or bays as they grow (235).

Management, habitat protection, and restoration continues to be inadequately funded (1488).  Lewis emphasized the need for nursery protection, restoring normal season water flows to estuaries, and habitat restoration as underutilized tools in snook fishery management.  Geographic information systems (GIS) technology is being used to assess changes in fisheries habitat, the effects of urbanization, and increasing fishing pressure on snook and other species (1486).

Efforts to restore wetlands were conducted, through wetland mitigation, water quality, and circulation improvements with a 1500 acre man made estuary in Broward County Fl (1474).  Snook abundance from 1986-1989 compared to 1992 did not increase.  Efforts to restore water quality in Tampa Bay resulted in reductions in nutrient input (1489).  The 1993 phytoplankton production was near half the rates measured in the early to mid 1980`s.  The recolonization of seagrass was minor.  A substantial reduction in fisheries yields may have resulted from the decrease in primary production.
Adult: Found in estuaries, Gulf passes, channels, beaches, river mouths, mangrove or salt marshes, ponds, brackish coastal waters, streams, and lakes (6 40 264 302 327 395 432 515 633 702 934 1303).  Reported in waters from 0.3 to 3.66 m in depth ranging in salinity from fresh water to euhaline (35 132 264 395).

Depth Distribution: Needs information.

sections.heading: WATER COLUMN HABITAT
sections.content:
Temperature: Very responsive to temperature with detrimental effects occurring at approximately 15 C or less (235 432).
Egg: No eggs have been observed in the wild, but they have been successfully spawned and developed at 28 C (404 636 734 1302 1309).  Experiments evaluated the development of eggs at 24, 26, 29 and 32 C (1490).  Development rates increased with increasing temperature.
Larvae: Larvae propagated in laboratories have been successfully raised at 24.6 to 32.4 C (404 636 734 1302) Larvae have been collected from Naples Bay, Florida in temperatures ranging from 28.7 to 31.4 C (1301).   In the laboratory all larvae reared at 24 C died (1490).  Statistical evaluation of developmental stages a t 26, 29, and 32 C indicated that 26 C resulted in the greatest larval growth and maximum yolk utilization efficiency.  The acute upper temperature tolerance of post-hatch larvae and the effects of initial acclimation temperature were investigated (1495).  Two day post-hatch larval mortalities increased from 30, 32, and 37 C, with 100% mortality at 34 C after 15 h. Similar results were found with 6-d post-hatch larvae.  Lower initial rearing temperatures resulted in lower maximum temperature tolerated.
Juvenile/Adult: Found in waters with a temperature range of 14.2 to 35.6 C (132 157 264 414 432 440 456 465 637 664 702).  In laboratory experiments, juveniles stopped feeding at 14.2 C, lost equilibrium at 12.7 C and died at 12.5 C (637).  More recent experiments found the lower lethal temperature for Florida snook ranged from 9 C in saltwater (19 %) to 10 C in freshwater (1408). The lower lethal limit for juveniles has been reported as 12 to 14 C, while that of adults probably approaches the lower end of a 6 to 13 C range suggesting adults are somewhat more tolerant of colder temperatures than fingerlings (236 264 432 637 664 1023 1068 1408).    McLaughlin et al. (1493) stated that juvenile snook did not seem to be adversely affected by colder water temperatures, which cause adult mortality.  Howells et al. (1408) suggested that other parameters (stock origin, food, salinity, and fish size) probably contributed to the differences in lower lethal temperatures observed in the various studies.  Numerous authors have reported snook as lethargic or stunned as a result of winter freezes (6 132 236 264 432 1023 1068). Gunter (253) reported that 6800 kg of snook and drum were killed near the southern tip of Texas during a severe winter in 1940, and Storey and Gudger (1068) listed snook as a species killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida.

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Egg/Larvae: Eggs and larvae have been raised in the lab in salinities from 30 to 38 % (404 636 734).  Both appear to prefer polyhaline to euhaline salinity ranges and are unable to develop in fresh water.  Larvae at 14 days of development can be successfully transferred to fresh water and are considered euryhaline at this point (6 636).  Snook larvae have been collected in Naples Bay, Fl at salinities ranging from 14.8 to 33.5 % (1301).  Salinities of >20 % are necessary to activate sperm for successful spawning (6 636).
Juvenile/Adult: Euryhaline, reported from a salinity range of 0.0 to 36 % (80 132 157 235 264 265 304 395 432 440 456 664 702 703).  On the Florida east coast, juveniles <50mm consistently occur at lower salinities whereas those >150mm are generally found in higher salinity habitats (235).  Snook are relatively widespread in freshwater (790) and have been collected in Lake Okeechobee (1313), coastal rivers (264 265), the Big Cypress Swamp (395), and at several locations in the Everglades (395 515 599 702).  Physiological studies of juveniles indicate they can osmoregulate at salinities between 0 and 45 % in a manner similar to other brackish water fishes (1311).  More than 70% of seine-caught and 90% of trawl-caught specimens taken in the Little Manatee River from 1988 to 1991 were taken at salinities <5 % (1492).  Maximum numbers were taken in October and November.  Changes in blood osmolality and gill morphology of juvenile snook after acclimation at various salinities (0, 15, 30, and 40 %) was investigated (1473).  The study found that juveniles quickly adapted to sudden changes in salinity.  The chloride cells in the gill appeared to be metabolically active regardless of salinity.

sections.heading: Dissolved Oxygen
sections.content:
Egg and Larvae: No information available.
Juvenile: Juvenile snook have been collected in impound wetland habitats associated with the Indian River Lagoon with D.O. levels of less than 1.0 mg/l (1271).  Peterson and Gilmore (1466) found an ontogenetic change in a juvenile snook`s ability to survive reduced oxygen levels, which correlated well with the habitat shift noted by Gilmore (235).  Small juveniles may also use aquatic surface respiration to utilize the well-oxygenated surface film during hypoxic events (1467).
Adult: No information available.
Turbidity: No data available.

sections.heading: Trophic Mode
sections.content:
Feeding (by life stage):
Food Items: (by life stage)
Larvae: Considered stenophagous.  Planktivore preying chiefly on copepods and their eggs and larvae.  Also feed on other invertebrate eggs, crab zoae, foraminifera, algae, and plant tissue (279).  Laboratory reared larvae began feeding when 2-3 days old and accepted rotifers, newly hatched Artemia, and copepod nauplii between 53 and 130 microns in size (1309).  Late post-larvae also feed on neonatal Gambusia (235 1309).
Juvenile: Data from wild-caught juveniles indicate that feeding occurs during the daytime (456).
 Smaller individuals have been reported as having eaten small copepods, amphipods, mysids, and zoaea and adults of palaemonid shrimp (80 235 279 456 664 1314 1491).  A feeding transition apparently occurs when juveniles are about 45mm long (456).  Snook become piscivorous at 25 to 30 mm TL with fish constituting the major portion of diet by 56 mm SL (279 636 664 1303).  Food organisms include: Anchoa mitchilli; Lagodon rhomboides; Gambusia affinis, Gambusia holbrooki, Cyprinodon variegatus; Palaemonetes spp., Penaeus spp., plant tissue, insects, and fish (235 279 456 1303 1491).  The predator-prey behavior of juvenile snook was studied in the laboratory (1491).
Adult: Diet consists mostly of fish and shrimp, but crabs, crayfish, and some plant tissue also utilized (279 432 1303 1314).  Fish constitute the most important component with the following reported from diet studies: Brevoortia sp., Eucinostomis sp., Mugil cephalus, Mugil sp., Lagodon rhomboides, Lagodon sp., Anchoa sp., Orthopristes chrysopterus, Poecilia latipinna, Gambusia affinis, Gambusia sp., and Molliensia sp. (80 432 515).

sections.heading: Mode
sections.content:
Domain: Snook spawn in higher saline estuarine and marine environments.  Fish ready to  spawn congregate in schools in shallow, saline, open waters just offshore in such areas as: river mouths, estuarine passes, along open beaches in the vicinity of inlets with actual spawning most likely in shallow nearshore waters (6 79 235 414 432 481 743).

Fertilization: Oviparous, external fertilization, sexes separate, exhibits sex reversal (1471).  Comparisons of the chromosomes of males and females did not show differences in chromosomatic size or number.  The banding patterns on the chromosomes supported the hypothesis of protandric hermaphroditisn.  Examination of more than 4,100 snook gonads confirmed that snook undergo sex reversal (1478).  For all snook <= 500 mm and < age 4 the sex ratio was skewed in favor of males (6.1 M:1.0 F), whereas for fish >= 800 mm and > age 7 the sex ratio favors females (1.0M: 3.2F).
Spawning Strategy:  broadcast spawner, eggs were most abundant in Tampa Bay during late evening and early morning hours (1499).
Reproductive Periodicity: Mating and spawning occurs in Florida from May to mid-November with peak spawning periods from June t o July along the southeast and southwest coasts and in August along the East central coast (6 235 432 456 481 734 743 1303). However, some spawning may occur year round in the warmer parts of the range. One female with roe reported from Corpus Christi, Texas in July (35); a ripe female was collected in early May in Haiti (40).

A diel and lunar sampling protocol was used to determine peak periods of various reproductive activities in Tampa Bay (1499).  Catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) and the gonadosomatic index (GSI) were highest during the new moon period of June and July.  Snook eggs from plankton samples were first present in Tampa Bay on June 7.

sections.heading: Seasonal Energetics
sections.content:
Parental Care: No guarding of eggs or larvae takes place (1499).
Maturation: Several studies have examined the sizes and ages of sexual maturity by sex of snook (327 432 600 788 1477).  Some snook mature by the end of the second year, but most are not mature until the end of the third year upon reaching a FL of 500 mm (432 743). The minimum reported sizes at maturity are 337 mm FL for females and 338 mm FL for males with approximately 50% mature at 400 mm and virtually all mature at 500 mm (432). The most comprehensive study found predicted sizes and ages at 50% maturity for east coast fish were males 379 mm at 2.3 yr, females 644 mm at 3.7 yr, and on the west coast males 401 mm at 1.9 yr, females 499 mm FL at 2.6 yr (1477)
Fecundity: Spawns large numbers of eggs; a 584 mm FL female contained ca. 1,440,000 eggs (743), and a 795mm female contained ca. 1,648,000 eggs (40).  Fecundity has been tentatively estimated at 45,000 eggs/lb body weight with some fractional spawning being reported (6 432).
Development (by life stage):

sections.heading: GROWTH
sections.content:
Length Range:(by life stage)
Egg: Fertilized eggs are 0.68-0.73 mm in diameter (6, 40, 404)
Larvae: At hatching 1.4 to 1.5 mm SL, increases to ca. 2.1 mm SL by 36 h after hatching (AH) (404). The larval stage ends at 13.8 to 16.4 mm SL, 34 days AH.

sections.heading: Young-Of-Year
sections.content:
Juvenile: Minimum size described 13.8 mm SL (404).  Juveniles are 163 mm FL at the end of the first winter (743).
Adult: The maximum size observed for male snook was 925 mm FL, and female snook was 1105 mm FL in Florida (1475).  Average size of adult is 91 cm TL with a weight of 4.5 kg, but can reach 1232 mm TL and 24.3 kg (327 788 600).

Gilmore et al. (235) gave the following equation for the length-weight relationship of juvenile snook based on measurements of 553 individuals:

sections.heading: Length At Age
sections.content:
Larvae: Growth rate for larvae varies.  Newly hatched larvae at 28+/-1 C grow 1.02 mm/day for a few hours, slowing rapidly to ca. 0.15 mm/day when about 2.4 mm SL.  Growth rate then increases gradually with increasing size from 0.15 to 0.50 mm/day in snook between 3.5-22.0 mm SL (404).
Juvenile: Recorded growth rate for juveniles in the wild is 0.5-1.2 mm/d (235 456) with a reported average of 0.6-0.7 mm/d for the first eight months of life (456).  Juveniles are 163 mm FL at the end of their first winter, and 342 mm FL by the end of their second (743).
Adult: The age and growth of snook was compared between the east and west coasts (1475).  Atlantic coast fish grow more quickly and reach a larger size sooner than snook on the Gulf coast.  The average size for males at age 13 was 812 mm FL on the east coast and 810 mm on the west coast of Florida  The average size for female snook was 1025 mm FL at age 18 on the east coast and 947 mm at age 19 on the west coast of Florida
Longevity:   Males live 13 yr, females 19 yr (1475).
Growth Equations: McMichael et al (456) found the following equations were good predictors of growth for summer-spawned juveniles:
[eq]
      A = 2.903488(L) - 0.024782(L^2) + 0.000096(L^3);   r^2 = 0.99
      	L = 0.008610(A^2) - 0.000025(A^3);                 r^2 = 0.99
[/eq]
where A is the age in days and L is standard length in mm.

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial: Important commercial fish in Central and South America, particularly in Mexico and Venezuela (791).  Never an important commercial species in the US, and in the early 20th century it was considered as barely edible (1294) and reported to be of little value at Key West (846).  By 1917, some fish were reaching commercial markets in the Fort Myers area where fish houses paid $.04/lb for snook (1068).  Demand developed early in Louisiana and in Texas it was considered as one of the important species in the 1930`s (35 432).  Caught on a small scale, Texas landings peaked at 105,451 lbs in 1928, and Florida landings peaked in 1948 at 800,698 lbs (432 446).  Declining numbers led to a ban on commercial landings in Florida in 1958 and to its virtual disappearance in Texas with the last commercially landed fish occurring there in 1961 (35 302 304 432 446 734 743).  Snook were taken infrequently by gill nets in Tampa bay (1494).
Recreational: Regarded as a popular sportfish, putting up spectacular fights as well as being good eating (6 35 327 432 440 633 736 734 743 788 791).  Readily accepts natural or artificial bait on hook and line; it is also caught by spearing (791).  Population declines since the 1930`s have resulted in this fish rarely being taken by sportsmen in Texas where it accounts for <1% of sport landings (304 446 734). Common snook landings in Florida in 1994 totaled 103,937 fish and were relatively evenly split between the Atlantic and Gulf coasts (1500).
Ecological Role: Considered a high trophic level carnivore feeding mostly on fish (279 636 664).  Juveniles use periferal habitats, including wetland impoundments, as nursery areas and may be an important transport mechanism to move energy out of these systems (235 1272).
Management Status: The commercial fishery for snook in Florida.ended in 1957, when the Florida Legislature banned all sales of snook, and granted the species gamefish status (1496).   The sport fishery is regulated through the Florida Marine Fisheries Commission (FMFC).  A saltwater recreational fishing license is required, if fishing from a boat at depths greater than four feet.  The holder of a marine sport fishing license and a snook stamp may land two snook per day.  Hatchery programs to enhance snook populations through stocking are discussed in the STOCK ENHANCEMENT description.
Species Stress: None.

sections.heading: Status
sections.content: Stock Status: Snook stocks on the east and west coasts of Florida have been increasing.

sections.heading: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
sections.content:
Induced Breeding: Collection of wild broodstock for hatchery production was accomplished on most days during the new moon (June-July) period (1504).  Success in induced spawning in Florida occurred during 1988 when the fish were captured in the afternoon after maturation of oocytes had commenced in wild-caught snook.

Six cell types have been identified in the adenohypophysis of adult snook (1505).  The somatotropic (STH) and gonadotropic (GTH) cells showed marked staining and morphological differences between winter and summer. Ager et al. (6) described the artificial spawning and development of Florida snook eggs and larvae during 1974 and 1975.  Maturation was induced using human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG).  Milt stored at 40 F up to 12 h was satisfactory for fertilization.  Injections of testosterone and leutenizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) during 1988 had some effect on maturation of males but not female snook in Texas (1506).  Attempts to induce maturation using increasing temperature (26 to 30 C) and increasing photoperiod (12h to 15h light period) in Texas were unsuccessful in inducing maturation (1507).  Attempts to induce maturation of snook maintained in cages in ponds were also unsuccessful (1508).

Three field spawning methods were tested in Florida during 1987 (1509).  Source spawning of fish captured early in the day and held in net pens resulted in 5 out of 143 fish spawned naturally. No fish spawned in net pens after field capture during the evening.  With fish given HCG injections, 2 out of 12 (16.7%) produced viable spawns.  Quasi-domesticated snook maintained on a long photoperiod (16 h) at 30 C ad 32 % salinity became mature and were spawned during 1989-91(1510).   Wild-caught fish maintained under the same conditions did not become sexually mature.  Stress minimization appeared to be the key to successful spawning.

A successful protocol for HCG-induced spawning of field-collected snook was developed in Florida during 1989 and 1990 (1514).  The most successful time was 32 to 34 h after HCG injection.  A seawater-free milt collection and storage system was developed.  The viability of eggs increased by obtaining eggs by excision rather than manual stripping of sexually mature adult snook.  Techniques for induced maturation and spawning were described by Roberts (1515).
Rearing: Lack of agitation of the water in rearing tanks during the first 6 h of incubation proved critical for consistent embryo development (6).   Hatching occurred from 24-30 h at temperatures between 82-87 F.  Poor fingerling survival precluded evaluation of reduced salinity on growth of juvenile snook in culture ponds in Texas during 1988 (1511).  Some fingerling production in Texas was achieved using fertilized eggs produced by FDNR with the eggs obtained from strip spawned broodfish (1512).  Eggs incubated at 27-29 C and 31-38 % for 2.5 d yielded 660,000 fry.  Some success was achieved by stocking fry into fertilized earthen ponds.  After 133 d, 1,665 fingerling snook averaging 133 mm TL were recovered for a survival rate of 53.7%.  Hence, snook fingerlings were produced in Texas ponds using techniques developed for rearing red drum.  Earlier studies in Florida have demonstrated excellent survival and growth of fingerling and subadult snook when stocked in sub-tropical freshwater ponds (1513).

Despite notable progress in producing fertilized eggs in Florida, the production of fry in large numbers by 1995 was still a hit and miss operation (1516).  The variable survival of different batches of fry may be due to a virus such as vibrato, or unknown water quality requirements.   It has been proposed that high larval mortalities may be due to a deficiency of unsaturated fatty acids (HUFAs) in the diets of culture fry (1517).
Feeding: An experiment was conducted with different diet combinations: 1) the algae Nannochloropsis oculata fed to rotifers; 2) Trochofeed (Pacific oyster trochophores); 3) Bioencapsulated food (oil emersion); 4) soybean meal; 5) Microfeast (modified fermentation product); and 6) zooplankton (collected wild).   Feeds were introduced when 50% of the larvae exhibited peristaltic movement.  Growth rates varied widely between replications of the same diet. The best growth 0.08 mm/d) occurred with the Nannochloropsis fed rotifer diet.  Ingredients that produced the best survival of larvae (5-7 d post-hatch) were the rotifer diet, bioencapsulation, soybean meal and trochophores.
Stocking: Due to the problems with producing juvenile snook in hatcheries, little or no research has been conducted to evaluate survival after stocking into marine environments.
Disease Control:   The monogenean, Rhabdosynochus rhabdosynochus present on the gills of adult snook broodstock was controlled by trichlorofon (dylox) at 1 mg/l (1469).  Rapid reinfestation of broodstock after treatment suggests that monogenean eggs may be resistant to the chemical.  A 5-7 d bath with 10 mg/l nitrofurazone promoted healing and inhibited bacterial growth and abrasions on hatchery held snook.

sections.heading: POPULATION
sections.content: Total Mortality: Total mortality (Z) and Actual mortality (A) rates have been determined from frequencies at age for common snook from Tampa Bay, and near Naples on the west coast, and from the Jupiter-Lake Worth Inlets on the east coast of Florida (1475, 1503).  The calculations derived from catch curves were done for the sexes separately and for the sexes combined.  The Z for Tampa Bay (1995) across ages 3-8 was 0.646 for the sexes combined (1503).  The Z for Naples Bay (1976-1981) across ages 4-8 was 0.687, and for the Jupiter-Lake Worth area (1995) was 0.476 across ages 6-14 for the sexes combined.  This is equivalent to Actual mortality rates (A) of 48% for Tampa Bay, 50% for Naples Bay, and 38% for Jupiter-Lake Worth.

sections.heading: Natural Mortality
sections.content: Fishing Mortality: No hooking mortality was noted with 23 adults monitored with ultrasonic transmitters (1483).  The hooking mortality was evaluated in terms of lure type, hook position, and water temperature (1487).  The total mortality out of 234 snook caught and released was 2.1%.  The mortalities from being hooked on the gill, hooked in the mouth, foul-hooked, and gut hooked were 0%, 0.81%, 0.21% and 17% respectively (R. Taylor, pers. comm. 1996).  No deaths were recorded for snook taken with lures.

sections.heading: Abundance By Month
sections.content:
Abundance By Year: The trend in recreational angler total-catch rates (CPUEs) has been upward since 1985 on the Atlantic coast, and since 1987 on the Gulf coast (1500).  The kept-catch rates have remained fairly stable since about 1985 on both coasts of Florida  Fishery independent estimates of common snook abundance in Tampa Bay and in Jupiter/West Palm Beach Inlets also indicate increasing trends since 1990 (1477).
Population Abundance: Tag-recapture methods were used to estimate trends in snook population abundance in Jupiter and Lake Worth inlets on the east coast, and in two microhabitats near Port Manatee in Tampa Bay on the west coast of Florida (1475).  East coast estimates were about 14,000 in 1990 and 1991, and then increased to 35,866 in 1992.  Length frequencies indicated a 16% increase on the east coast during 1992.

sections.heading: Annual Cohort Success
sections.content:
Management Regulations (by state and federal):
Florida: A decline in sport catches in the late 1970`s and early 1980`s and tagging data indicating a population decline, induced the Florida Legislature to grant emergency power to the Florida Dept. of Nat. Res. (FDNR) in 1982 to institute a closed season on the sport fishery.  Stringent management in recent years, combined with mild winters, may have influenced increases in snook abundance.   Current Florida laws include a closed season from 15 December through January and during June-August, a minimum 24� TL, a 2 fish bag limit, and allow possession of only one fish larger than 34�TL.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Competition: Interactions with other species include habitat overlapping and parasitism.  Possible competition may exist between snook and associated fish such as Megalops atlanticus, Elops saurus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Bairdiella chrysoura, and Centropristes ocyurus (414).

sections.heading: Predation
sections.content: Parasites/Diseases:  An unidentified nematode has been reported parasitizing the mesentery and stomach wall of snook, but apparently with no ill effects (432).  Other reported parasites are Philometra centropomi in the nasal mucosa (633) and Prosthenhystera obesa in the gall bladder (1312).  Snook have also been identified as a host for Lymphocystis virus (633).  Gill ectoparasites have also been described (1308).  Three species of myxosporidian parasites found in snook are Myxobolus centropomi (n. sp.), Ceratomyxa choleospora (n. sp.), and Fabeospora sp.(1468).  Other parasites found on snook include a monogenean (Rhabdosynochus rhabdosynochus), digenean (Lecithochirium microstomum), nematodes (Dichelyne spinicaudatus, Contracaecum spiculigerum),  and a copepod (Caligulus pretextus).

sections.heading: Eutrophication
sections.content: Pollutant Toxicity: Environmental factors are believed to have played a large role in addition to fishing mortality in the decline in snook populations in various areas of Florida (432 1496 1497 1498).  Environmental alterations and degradations include reduced freshwater inflow to estuaries, sewage and industrial pollution, dredging and filling, mosquito control practices and pesticide use.  Malathion and baytex, pesticides commonly used in mosquito control, were found to be toxic to snook eggs and larvae (1498).  There were birth defects in larvae exposed to malathion.
